passage: I'm Neelam, Jyoti's neighbour, and we played hide-and-seek in her flat on Sunday. Round one, Jyoti hid behind the door, and I found her before I'd finished counting in my head. Round two, she went behind the long curtain; her toes gave her away, but it took me longer. Round three, she was under the bed, flat as a mat, and I gave up. I don't know if she planned it, but each hiding place got better.

qa.q: Where did Jyoti hide in round three?
qa.a: She was under the bed, flat as a mat.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling when she gave up in round three?
qa.a: Neelam was surprised and impressed, noticing that each hiding place got better.

qa.q: What else could Jyoti try to hide even better?
qa.a: She could think about where Neelam searched last time and pick somewhere Neelam hasn't looked yet.

qa.q: What might Jyoti be feeling after winning round three?
qa.a: She is probably delighted and proud after being found fast twice.

grounding: An observer describes a child who is found quickly behind the door, then tries the curtain and the bed, learning which spots work.

passage:
Monday: Dhruv hid behind the bedroom door. Sunaina found him before she reached ten. He groaned.
Tuesday: he picked the curtain. Sunaina walked past twice before seeing his feet. "Almost!"
Thursday: he slid under the bed and held still. Sunaina searched the door, the curtain, and gave up. Dhruv crawled out, dusty and grinning. "The bed's the best."

qa.q: Where did Dhruv hide on Tuesday?
qa.a: He picked the curtain.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling when he crawled out on Thursday?
qa.a: He was proud and happy that the bed finally worked.

qa.q: What else could Dhruv try next time Sunaina seeks?
qa.a: He could pick a new spot again, since Sunaina may now check under the bed first.

qa.q: How does the change look to Sunaina?
qa.a: Sunaina finds Dhruv harder to find each day and may feel a bit frustrated and impressed.

grounding: Over several days a child moves from the door to the curtain to under the bed, learning from being found which spots work.

passage: Last summer in Seville, cousin Ulla had won hide-and-seek by squeezing into Grandma's big wardrobe. This year Pablo remembered. When his friend Mateo began counting, Pablo ran straight to the wardrobe, pulled the door almost shut and crouched among the coats. Mateo, who hadn't been there last summer, searched the kitchen and the garden. Ulla walked past and winked. Pablo stayed hidden until Mateo gave up.

qa.q: Where did Pablo crouch?
qa.a: He crouched among the coats in the wardrobe.

qa.q: What was Pablo feeling as he stayed hidden?
qa.a: He was probably excited and pleased that Ulla's trick was working for him.

qa.q: What else could Pablo try when playing with Ulla?
qa.a: He would need a new spot, because Ulla knows the wardrobe trick and would look there first.

qa.q: How does the wardrobe trick look to Ulla?
qa.a: Ulla recognises her own trick and is amused, winking because she knows Mateo won't guess.

grounding: A child hides in the wardrobe because an older cousin won there before, and it works only because the seeker doesn't know the trick.

passage: In the community centre crèche, the steel almirah held the nap mats. Last week Wasim's cousin Naveen had won by hiding inside it. Today the new helper, Kiran didi, was seeking. Wasim tiptoed in and crouched on the mats, leaving the door open a crack. Kiran didi checked under tables, behind the curtain. She never looked in the almirah. Naveen, sitting out, smirked. Wasim giggled into his knees.

qa.q: What did the steel almirah hold?
qa.a: It held the nap mats.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling as he giggled into his knees?
qa.a: He was excited and pleased to be copying Naveen's winning spot.

qa.q: What else could Wasim try if Naveen were seeking?
qa.a: He would need a new spot, because Naveen knows the almirah trick and would look there straight away.

qa.q: How does Naveen see Wasim's hiding place?
qa.a: Naveen knows the trick is his own and finds it funny that the new helper doesn't know it.

grounding: A child hides in the almirah because his cousin won there before, and it works only because the new seeker doesn't know the trick.

passage: Behind the sofa in the Oslo flat, Emil crouched and listened. Tuan was counting by the window. "Eight, nine, ten! Coming!" Emil peeked round the side. If Tuan walks left, I'll go right, he thought. Tuan's socks padded left. Emil slid right, around the far arm of the sofa, and stayed low. Tuan looked behind the sofa, found nothing and scratched his head.

qa.q: Where was Tuan counting?
qa.a: Tuan was counting by the window.

qa.q: What was Emil thinking as he peeked round the side?
qa.a: He was alert and a little nervous, planning to go right if Tuan went left.

qa.q: What would you change in Emil's plan if Tuan turned back?
qa.a: He could watch again and move the other way, since his rule depends on Tuan's move.

qa.q: How does the sofa look to Tuan?
qa.a: Tuan is puzzled, because he checks behind it and finds nothing.

grounding: A child makes a simple if-then plan about which way the seeker goes around the sofa and moves the other way.

passage: At the community centre's rainy-day play hour, Siddharth crouched behind the long sofa in the reading corner. Zubin was seeking. Siddharth held his breath and whispered to himself, "If he goes by the shelves, I go by the window." Zubin's trainers squeaked toward the shelves. Siddharth crawled the other way, around the far end. Zubin reached the spot where Siddharth had been and found only a cushion.

qa.q: What did Zubin find behind the sofa?
qa.a: He found only a cushion.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling as Zubin's trainers squeaked closer?
qa.a: He was probably tense and excited, ready to move the other way.

qa.q: What else could Siddharth do if Zubin comes round both ends?
qa.a: He could pick a new hiding place altogether, since his rule only works if Zubin chooses one side.

qa.q: If you were Zubin, what would you think?
qa.a: You would feel puzzled that the spot was empty, and might start guessing that Siddharth is moving around.

grounding: A child plans "if the seeker goes one way, I go the other" around a sofa and uses it to stay hidden.

subtype: Approach: simple step list as seeker [Action]
passage: "Ready!" called Gargi from somewhere in the Mumbai flat. Joseph uncovered his eyes and set off. Bedroom first: under the bed, behind the door. No Gargi. Kitchen next: under the table, beside the fridge. No. Balcony: behind the plant pots. Empty. He didn't go back. He went on to the bathroom, pulled the curtain, and there she was in the tub. "Found you!"

qa.q: Where did Joseph find Gargi?
qa.a: In the tub, behind the bathroom curtain.

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling when he pulled the curtain?
qa.a: He was excited and pleased that his room-by-room search worked.

qa.q: What else could Joseph add to his search?
qa.a: He could check the most likely hiding places first in each room, so the search is faster.

qa.q: How might Gargi see Joseph's search?
qa.a: Gargi probably heard him move steadily closer, room by room, which may have made her nervous and excited.

grounding: A child seeks by checking rooms in a fixed order so no place is searched twice.

subtype: Approach: simple step list as seeker [Action]
passage:
"Deepak, where are you?" Irfan shouted.
No answer.
"Okay. Bedroom first." He looked under the bed. "Not here."
"Kitchen now." He opened the cupboard under the sink. "No."
"Balcony." He peered behind the drying rack. "Not there."
"Irfan, you already checked the bedroom," Ammi said.
"I know! I'm not going back. Bathroom's last." He yanked the door. "Found you, Deepak!"

qa.q: Where did Irfan look in the kitchen?
qa.a: He opened the cupboard under the sink.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling when he said "I'm not going back"?
qa.a: He felt sure and determined about his order, not wanting to search the same place twice.

qa.q: What else could Irfan try when seeking?
qa.a: He could listen for giggles as he goes, since sounds could cut his search short.

qa.q: How does Irfan's search look to Deepak?
qa.a: Deepak hears Irfan's voice moving closer room by room, and is probably a bit nervous and excited.

grounding: A child seeks by checking rooms in a fixed order: bedroom, kitchen, balcony, bathroom, so nowhere is searched twice.

passage: The cousins had only ten minutes before the bus, so the game was quick. Tarun counted fast. Sonali didn't run. She stood right beside the dining table, squeezed her eyes shut and puffed up her cheeks, holding her breath. If I don't breathe, he can't see me, she thought. Tarun opened his eyes and burst out laughing. "Sonali, you're right there!" She let out her breath in a whoosh, red-faced.

qa.q: How long did the cousins have before the bus?
qa.a: They had only ten minutes.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling when she let out her breath, red-faced?
qa.a: She was embarrassed and surprised to be found so easily.

qa.q: What would help Sonali next time?
qa.a: Finding a real hiding place, like under the table, since holding her breath does not hide her.

qa.q: How does Sonali's plan look to Tarun?
qa.a: To Tarun it looks funny because she is standing in plain view.

grounding: A child holds her breath and squeezes her eyes shut, sure she is invisible while standing in the open, so wishing replaces a plan.

passage: Swati stood in the middle of the colony park, eyes squeezed shut, cheeks puffed, not breathing. Her brother Lalit was counting under the gulmohar. "Twenty! Coming!" He turned and there she was, three steps away, trembling. "Swati, I can see you." She burst out breathing. "You can't! I was invisible!" Lalit laughed. She stamped her foot and looked close to tears.

qa.q: Where was Lalit counting?
qa.a: He was counting under the gulmohar.

qa.q: What was Swati feeling when she stamped her foot?
qa.a: She was frustrated and hurt, sure she had been invisible and upset to be laughed at.

qa.q: What else could Swati try next round?
qa.a: She could hide behind the slide or a tree, a real hiding place rather than a wish.

qa.q: How might Lalit's laugh feel to Swati?
qa.a: It stings, because she believed her plan and he found it funny.

grounding: A child holds her breath and shuts her eyes, sure she is invisible in the open, and is upset when found at once.

passage: At the playschool's indoor hour, Kavitha was found first again: third round in a row. Siddharth, the seeker, cheered. Kavitha's chin wobbled, but she didn't cry. She stood up straight and said, "One more. Then I seek and you hide." Siddharth thought about it. "Okay, one more." This time Kavitha didn't even try a new spot. She waited behind the same bookcase, already planning her counting.

qa.q: How many rounds in a row was Kavitha found first?
qa.a: Three rounds.

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling when her chin wobbled?
qa.a: She was disappointed and hurt at being found first again.

qa.q: What else could Kavitha try besides changing the rules?
qa.a: She could also try a new hiding place, since swapping to seeker doesn't teach her where to hide.

qa.q: How might Siddharth see Kavitha's deal?
qa.a: Siddharth probably thinks it's fair and is happy to keep the game going.

grounding: A child found first three times changes the rules of the game instead of her hiding place.

passage: I'm Leela, Sahil's big cousin, and I was seeking at Nani's house. I found Sahil first in round one, behind the fridge. Round two, behind the fridge again. Round three, under the table. His lip went out. Then he said, "One more, and then I seek and you hide." I agreed. He didn't try a new spot; he just hid again and got found. But he looked much happier knowing his turn to seek was coming.

qa.q: Where did Leela find Sahil in round three?
qa.a: Under the table.

qa.q: What was Leela feeling when she agreed to Sahil's deal?
qa.a: Leela felt kind and a little amused, happy to let Sahil have his turn.

qa.q: What else could help Sahil in the next hiding round?
qa.a: He could try a spot he hasn't used, since changing the rules doesn't change his hiding.

qa.q: What might the deal mean for Sahil?
qa.a: It gives him hope and a way out of losing, which seems to make him feel better.

grounding: An observer describes a child found first three times who bargains to seek next, changing the rules rather than his hiding place.

passage: In the kindergarten corner, Amandeep sat Mridul on a cushion. "Okay, you're sick. Your tummy hurts. I'll listen to your heart, then I'll give you medicine." She held a pretend stethoscope to her doll first. "Breathe in. Good. Now you say ow." "Ow," said the doll, in her voice. "Now you, Mridul." Mridul giggled and said, "Ow!"

qa.q: Where did Amandeep sit Mridul?
qa.a: She sat Mridul on a cushion.

qa.q: What was Amandeep thinking as she tried it on the doll first?
qa.a: She felt eager and serious, practising the lines so the real game would go right.

qa.q: What else could Amandeep do to plan the game?
qa.a: She could ask Mridul which role to play, so the plan fits both of them.

qa.q: How does the game look to Mridul?
qa.a: Mridul finds it funny and fun, giggling and playing along.

grounding: A child rehearses a doctor game ahead of time, saying the steps and acting out the first lines with a doll.

passage: I'm Kiran, and Vishal is my classmate's little brother. At their house I watched him set up a pretend clinic. He whispered to a teddy, "You're sick. I listen to your heart. Then medicine." He pressed a bottle cap to its chest and said, "Breathe!" Then he whispered it all again. I think he was practising before his sister came, but maybe he just liked talking to the teddy.

qa.q: What did Vishal press to the teddy's chest?
qa.a: He pressed a bottle cap to its chest.

qa.q: What was Kiran thinking as Vishal whispered it all again?
qa.a: Kiran was curious and unsure, wondering if Vishal was practising or just enjoying talking to the teddy.

qa.q: What else could help Vishal plan the game?
qa.a: He could ask his sister what she wants to be, so the game fits them both.

qa.q: How might Vishal feel when his sister arrives?
qa.a: He would probably feel ready and excited, because he already practised the lines.

grounding: An observer watches a child rehearse a doctor game out loud with a teddy before playing it.

passage: On the mud-floor verandah of their home in Bijapur, Pooja and her brother Varun planned their clinic. "You're the patient, I'm the doctor," said Pooja. Varun nodded. Pooja fetched the toy stethoscope from the tin box. Varun found an old strip of cloth for a bandage. Then they laid a gunny sack on the floor for the bed. Only when everything was ready did Varun lie down and say, "My arm hurts."

qa.q: What did they use for the bed?
qa.a: A gunny sack on the floor.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling as he lay down?
qa.a: He seemed happy and ready, pleased that the clinic was set up.

qa.q: What would you change first if the set-up took too long?
qa.a: They could start with just the stethoscope and add props as they play, so the game doesn't stall.

qa.q: How does the set-up look to Varun?
qa.a: Varun seems content to follow Pooja's plan and help find props.

grounding: Two children assign roles, gather props and set up a clinic before starting to play.

passage: On the balcony of their Haifa flat, Noa and her friend Dalia got ready. "I'm the doctor, you're the nurse," Noa said. They fetched the toy stethoscope from the toy box and a roll of gauze from Noa's craft drawer. Dalia spread a towel over the cushion. "This is the bed." Noa lined up two plastic spoons as medicine. "Now," she said, "we can start."

qa.q: What did Dalia spread over the cushion?
qa.a: She spread a towel over the cushion.

qa.q: What was Noa feeling when she said "Now we can start"?
qa.a: She felt satisfied and ready now everything was set up.

qa.q: What else could the girls add to their plan?
qa.a: They could decide who the patient is, since both have jobs but no one is sick yet.

qa.q: How does the set-up look to Dalia?
qa.a: Dalia seems glad to help and enjoys preparing the bed.

grounding: Two children assign roles, gather props and set up a pretend clinic before starting the game.

passage:
"I'm the doctor!" Kunal grabbed the toy stethoscope.
"No, me!" Baljeet pulled it back toward his chest.
"I said first!"
"I want to!"
Both stood holding one end.
Kunal let go. "Okay. You be doctor first. I'm doctor next game."
Baljeet stared. "Promise?"
"Promise."
"Okay! Lie down, you're sick."
Kunal lay down on his back, grinning.

qa.q: What did both boys want to be?
qa.a: The doctor.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling when he let go of the stethoscope?
qa.a: He was ready to share, maybe a bit disappointed but keen to start the game.

qa.q: What else could the boys try to share the role?
qa.a: They could take turns within one game, since both still want to be the doctor.

qa.q: How does the deal look to Baljeet?
qa.a: Baljeet is surprised and pleased, and wants a promise to be sure it's fair.

grounding: Two children both want to be doctor, and one offers turns so play can begin without a fight.

passage:
Note for Jaya's parents
During free play, Jaya and Omkar both wanted to be the doctor. They each gripped the plastic stethoscope. Before I stepped in, Jaya said, "You be doctor first. I'll be doctor in the next game." Omkar let out a breath and agreed. They played happily, and when the bell rang Jaya reminded him, "My turn next time." I praised her idea at pickup.

qa.q: What did Jaya say to Omkar?
qa.a: She said, "You be doctor first. I'll be doctor in the next game."

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling when she reminded Omkar of her turn?
qa.a: She felt hopeful and determined that the deal would be kept.

qa.q: What else could Jaya try if Omkar forgets the deal?
qa.a: She could ask an adult to help remember the turns, so the deal stays fair.

qa.q: How might Omkar see Jaya's offer?
qa.a: Omkar seems relieved and happy, letting out a breath and agreeing.

grounding: A teacher's note describes a child who offers turns at being doctor so play can begin without a fight.

passage: Aditi's cousins were arriving in ten minutes, and her doctor game needed a costume. "Mumma, do you have an old dupatta?" Mumma pulled a faded blue one from the trunk. "Here. And if you fold it like this," she twisted a corner, "it's a nurse's cap." Aditi gasped. Her brother Dhruv wanted one too, so Mumma folded the rest into a sling. The doorbell rang.

qa.q: How long before the cousins arrived?
qa.a: Ten minutes.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling when she gasped?
qa.a: She was delighted and excited by Mumma's idea for the nurse's cap.

qa.q: What else could Aditi try if Mumma had no dupatta?
qa.a: She could make a cap from paper, since the idea of a costume matters more than the cloth.

qa.q: How does the costume idea look to Dhruv?
qa.a: Dhruv wants to join in, so the sling feels like his share of the fun.

grounding: A child asks her mother for an old dupatta as a costume, and the mother supplies it and suggests it can become a nurse's cap.

passage: Tushar and his friend Yogesh were playing hospital in the Pune flat. "We need a costume," Tushar said. He ran to the kitchen. "Aai, can I have an old dupatta?" Aai pulled a faded pink one from the cupboard. "You could fold it to make a nurse's cap," she said, folding it for him. Tushar ran back and wore it. Yogesh stared. "Where did you get that?"

qa.q: What colour was the dupatta?
qa.a: It was faded pink.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling when he ran back wearing it?
qa.a: He was proud and excited about his new costume.

qa.q: What could Tushar try next time?
qa.a: He could ask Aai for a second prop so Yogesh has a costume too.

qa.q: How does Yogesh see Tushar's costume?
qa.a: Yogesh is surprised and perhaps a little jealous, asking where it came from.

grounding: A child asks his mother for an old dupatta, and she suggests folding it into a nurse's cap.
